findings_qualitative.value: High-velocity CO (up to ±400 km/s) is consistent with a bipolar outflow nearly perpendicular to the nuclear disk, with possible rotation in the p-v diagram.

evidence.quote: Higher-velocity emission (up to $\pm 400$ km s$^{-1}$) is consistent with a bipolar outflow

claims.hypothesis: CO emission traces a bipolar outflow from the torus
claims.experiment: Velocity-binned maps and spectroastrometry with a 5-degree-tilt bicone simulation
claims.result: Blue and red peaks are displaced 1.2 pc along an axis ~78 deg to the maser line
claims.finding: The high-velocity CO is consistent with a bipolar outflow along the AGN axis

evidence.quote: the high-velocity CO emission is consistent with a bipolar outflow along the AGN axis

claims.hypothesis: The CO velocity field also contains rotation
claims.experiment: p-v diagram compared with an illustrative Keplerian disk model
claims.result: Elongated components match the maser chain and a shallower slope
claims.finding: Kinematics are consistent with rotation plus outflow, i.e. a disk wind

evidence.quote: The overall similarity with the data suggests the presence of rotation on top of the radial outflow

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: A collimated jet explanation of the p-v elongated features was judged unlikely.

evidence.quote: The existence of two such features with different slopes and the overlap of one of them with the maser line make a jet-based explanation unlikely

limitations_admitted.value: Single CO transition makes it hard to constrain cloud physical parameters.

evidence.quote: Having detected a single CO transition, it is difficult to derive strong constraints on the physical parameters of emitting clouds.
